EUROPE’s gasoil prices have climbed to one of the highest levels on record even after adjusting for inflation. Front-month gasoil futures have averaged more than €1270 per tonne so far in September, the third highest on record after October and June 2022, and higher than during the oil price spike in 2008. The continued disruption of crude and fuel exports through the Strait of Hormuz combined with Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s oil refineries and the relative weakness of the euro against the dollar have all contributed to near-record high prices. The threat of an outright ban or restrictions on U.S. diesel exports has intensified the upward pressure:

EIA reported in its petroleum supply monthly today that US crude oil production hit 13.948 million b/d. 

But if you look at the adjustment, it was -0.469 million b/d, which implies that US crude oil production was overstated. 

Effective production is 13.479 million b/d. 

This is the 3rd consecutive month of negative supply adjustment.

EIA reported materially lower refinery throughput than our estimate contributing to the delta (16.257 vs 16.7, 3.1 million bbls). 

Meanwhile, lower refinery throughput is translating to much lower product storage. 

Given how low inventories are today, we have no cushion left.

September produced a striking divergence between #gold and investment demand. Gold fell as US Treasury #yields surged, yet gold ETF holdings rose for a second consecutive month. The continued inflows suggest investors were looking beyond the immediate headwind from higher real yields and instead focusing on what those higher borrowing costs may ultimately mean for fiscal sustainability and already elevated government debt levels. It raises an interesting question: what happens to gold once yields stabilise and the inflationary impulse from higher energy prices begins to fade? If investment demand has remained resilient during such a hostile rates environment, an easing of that pressure could provide a powerful tailwind. 
Chart source: Bloomberg
